title: The Seattle chocolate scene is like the river in Willy Wonka factory
text: The Seattle chocolate scene is like the river in Willy Wonka’s factory | The Seattle Times Skip to content By Jackie Varriano Seattle Times food writer Seattle’s rich chocolate scene is like the river in Willy Wonka’s factory — a bubbling, swiftly moving current. So, who’s along for the ride? There have been high-profile shake-ups and departures of late: Theo Chocolate — one of the first bean-to-bar makers in town — has left Seattle entirely, closing its last Fremont retail shop in February . In March, Seattle Chocolate debuted a new name and look, rebranding as Maeve after three decades. Meanwhile, a fan-favorite shop announced it will leave Pioneer Square. There are also new, smaller players making chocolate from scratch (and expanding their operations), like a new bean-to-bar shop that will open in Greenwood at the end of April. Here’s the scoop on the state of the Emerald City chocolate scene in 2025. MORE FOOD & DRINK 2025 James Beard finalists include 3 WA chefs and restaurants Skagit Valley tulips are back for 2025. Try 3 lunch ideas on your trip Seattle Restaurant Week’s best deals — our critic’s top 10 picks WA ranchers deeply love their cattle, from birth to burger 32 new Seattle restaurants to try this spring ‘Seattle Eats’: Toasting restaurants we lost recently — and new ones, too More City with a sweet tooth First: a chocolate lesson. Confectioners mainly take premade chocolate from a manufacturer and melt it to make truffles and other treats. A bean-to-bar chocolate maker, on the other hand, takes beans from the cacao tree and roasts them, grinding the fermented beans in a chocolate-refining machine, turning them into a smooth, thick ribbon of chocolate. Then comes the sugar, cocoa liquor or butter, or even mix-ins like rose petals, pop rocks or toffee chips. Advertising Seattle was a confectioner’s hub for decades: Almond Rocas have been made at the Brown & Haley factory in Tacoma for more than a century, while Frango mints were created at a Frederick & Nelson department store in 1918. But Seattle has increasingly become a chocolate-making town instead of a chocolate-melting one. Chocolate makers treat chocolate like coffee or wine, where factors like soil composition, topography and microclimate impact the finished bar. Good chocolate shouldn’t just taste like sugar — and it’s not always overly sweet, either. Chocolate can be nutty or smoky, malted or fruity, even when the only ingredient is cacao. The making isn’t the hardest part — it’s knowing how to treat the beans, how to blend them, how to temper properly. That’s what makes specialty chocolate look and taste special. Still, there’s always the question if a $12 bar of chocolate is “worth it” when a Hershey’s bar costs $2. It’s not a new question. When Fran Bigelow opened the first location of her legendary Seattle confections company, Fran’s, in Madison Valley in 1982, she was educating every customer who came through the doors about European chocolate, the differences in taste and technique. “A high-quality chocolate experience wasn’t common,” said Andrina Bigelow, who joined her mom’s business in 2007 and is now its CEO. “We still make things on a very small scale. And you still need to explain to people why the cost difference is there, but once they try it, these are loyal customers.” Fran Bigelow began making truffles in the early ’80s, when Andrina would hand out sweets to customers. Before long, truffles started outselling their chocolate cakes. Things exploded in 1986, when Bigelow started making caramel and introduced the Gold Bar — a chocolate-covered confection with caramel and nuts. Bigelow sent a few confections to Chuck Williams, founder of Williams Sonoma, saying, “The world is ready for an adult candy bar.” Williams agreed and began selling Gold Bars nationally. The rest is history. Advertising While the Bigelow family business — including Andrina and her brother, Director of Chocolate Dylan Bigelow, who joined Fran’s in 2001 — has been going strong for four-plus decades, the Seattle chocolate scene picked up more steam when Theo Chocolate, the city’s first bean-to-bar maker, set up shop in Fremont in 2005. Theo was sold to American Licorice Company in 2023, which closed both of the brand’s remaining retail shops in February. Still, Theo signaled a change in the chocolate river’s flow — from confectioners to chocolatiers. Changing directions When Jean Thompson took over Seattle Chocolate in 2001, she didn’t know much about the product “besides eating it.” Originally an investor, Thompson saw that Seattle Chocolate was in trouble, so she jumped in with both feet. She didn’t like what she found while checking out the competition at the grocery store. “In order to convey you were chocolate, you had to put (all packaging) in earth tones. Everything was brown,” Thompson said. “And everyone targeted men — ads were all sexy women offering chocolate to men. We wanted to target women.” She introduced bold, bright packaging and formed relationships with farms in Peru, Ecuador, the Dominican Republic, Tanzania and West Africa, committing to ethical sourcing practices. In 2024, the business added chocolate-making to its repertoire. Advertising “We now make our own dark chocolate where we source the chocolate liquor and turn it into our flavor profile by blending beans,” Thompson said. And she remains open to change. When Ellie Thompson came to her mom with a proposition three years ago, she was receptive to the tough feedback. “She said (Seattle Chocolate) isn’t cool anymore,” Jean said. “Things get stale, they get staid. People like it, but you can’t make it into the future.” Most Read Life Stories On Mother’s Day, Seattle-area moms give advice to their younger selves Emma Chamberlain wears custom-painted Mugler gown at the Met Gala Why travelers are ditching their bags at the airport Unpacking recent research on artificial sweeteners. Should we use them? Looking for an instant crowd-pleaser? Try these turkey Reuben sliders In March, the 34-year-old company became Maeve, with the name and packaging overhauled. While Seattle Chocolate was colorful, it was understated about the company itself. Maeve, named after an Irish warrior queen, promotes its values on the label. “Chocolate has evolved to meet consumers where they are at,” Ellie Thompson said. “Gen Z and millennials lead with values, and we needed to show receipts about where (our chocolate) is from and where it’s made.” Though the name has changed, “it’s the same on the inside,” Jean said. “The same melt-away center, the same commitments. We’re still Rainforest Alliance, women-owned, carbon-neutral.” Sponsored The Van Arsdale brothers of Spinnaker Chocolate, Kelly and Chris, have committed their family to the chocolate business, too. The Van Arsdales started in Chris’ garage in Santa Cruz, Calif., spending years making chocolate, building “his garage into a mini-factory,” said Kelly Van Arsdale. “It was a hobby that never went away.” Friends told the brothers they should sell the chocolate, so they began looking for a commercial space in 2019. The day they were supposed to sign the paperwork, though, Kelly’s pregnant wife was laid off, and it felt like the “universe was telling us to pause.” That break would eventually lead to Seattle. “San Francisco has so many chocolate companies — really big ones and really small ones,” Kelly said. “I felt like it was going to be tough to stand out when we were there. It was a blessing my wife got let go the day she did — could you imagine if it was one day later?” The Van Arsdales eventually packed up, moved to Seattle, renovated a house, had a baby and found a retail location. They opened Spinnaker Chocolate in Bryant in 2021, and now the family is preparing to open a brand-new retail shop, cafe and chocolate factory in Fremont this spring. The Van Arsdales were ready to explain a lot when they opened — “why people should choose craft chocolate over a big, industrial chocolate maker,” and why a bar at Spinnaker can cost $12. Advertising Well, here’s why: This chocolate is light-years away from your average grocery store bar, in taste and price. Hershey’s makes 373 million signature milk chocolate bars per year, while Spinnaker makes around 100,000 bars’ worth of chocolate in total annually. Place a square of Spinnaker’s 70% dark chocolate Vanuatu bar on your tongue and your taste buds go on a journey. There are hints of dried fruit and a subtle smokiness, but the only ingredients are cacao and sugar. All those flavors come directly from the cacao and how it was roasted and finished. “We’re all trying to do the same thing: elevate craft chocolate in general,” Kelly Van Arsdale said. “Even if we convinced 1% of people to move away from industrial chocolate, that’s a massive amount of people, and we’re all working together.” Aaron Lindstrom runs a chocolate operation with a musical flourish at Cocoa Legato, set to open at the end of April. He said, “Chocolate is a beautiful luxury item.” Lindstrom is a musician and a longtime former Theo employee who helped overhaul the tour experience in 2019, penning a 70-page book that showcased the journey of cacao from farm to finished dessert. Lindstrom left the company before the merger with American Licorice Company; within a few months, he was dreaming up Cocoa Legato. Planned to open April 26 on the corner of Greenwood and 85th Street, Cocoa Legato is a bean-to-bar chocolatier that sources beans primarily from Colombia — where Lindstrom was born — as well as Peru. They make the bars on-site from start to finish. Advertising “I got the passion (for chocolate) while at Theo and I’m also a full-time musician,” he said. “My whole world is chocolate and music.” Lindstrom’s shiny bars, like a Colombian chocolate with well-balanced fruity notes, are stamped to look like a record. The cafe also has a stage, with plans for live music in the evenings, and each bar of chocolate gets paired with a local musician. Andrina Bigelow of Fran’s says all this change — new chocolate makers coming up, others moving around — has been exciting to see over the years. It was hard when her mom started the business on her lonesome. “But the more people that are paying attention and talking about sourcing and quality and how to taste chocolate and enjoy it,” Andrina Bigelow said, is all “the better.” Bittersweet departure While Cocoa Legato and Spinnaker expand, some chocolate makers are leaving Seattle entirely. In February, Intrigue Chocolate chef and co-owner Aaron Barthel announced that he and partner Karl Mueller are moving the brand to Minnesota. A blog post explained that “while we love making and sharing chocolate in the Pacific Northwest, this next chapter brings us closer to family and allows us to realize a dream we’ve nurtured for years — owning our own building that will house both our chocolate factory and our upstairs apartment.” Advertising Barthel, who has been making chocolate under the Intrigue name since 2005, started with truffles, making the desserts for friends who owned a catering company. He said “people knew Frango and Dilettante and Fran’s, but there was no such thing as craft chocolate” in Seattle at the time, Barthel said. “Theo started the same year we did and that was regionally a big eye-opener for people.” In 2017, Barthel started making his own chocolate, using a couple of tabletop mills to refine the chocolate and breaking up the pieces to sell to coffee shops for drinks. “A few years later, we switched to medallions, free-forming the medallions and adding dried cherries or barberries or other fun things on top,” Barthel said. “About five years ago, we moved into making them as bars.” These days, Barthel said expectations from customers are broader. People are familiar with words like “single origin” and might even have an idea of what regions or percentages of cacao they like. Leaving Seattle is bittersweet, in part because of those repeat conversations with longtime customers. But, after 15 years in business in Pioneer Square, Barthel says the reality is that while rents go up, “walk-in retail business does not.” “In a time when there was a lot more foot traffic that worked,” he said, “but foot traffic isn’t going back up.” There won’t be a retail shop in the new space in Chisholm, Minn., allowing Barthel to focus on chocolate-making, running just a web store and spending time with his aging parents. People will still be able to find Intrigue online — even now, Barthel is busy making as much chocolate as possible to get them through the move. “We realized being small could also be a really healthy business size,” he said. “And that at a smaller size and with the movement of the customer base online, that place was more agnostic. We could be more flexible with location.” Jackie Varriano : Jackie Varriano is a food writer at The Seattle Times who covers neighborhood restaurants around Western Washington, reporting on the ways food and communities intersect.
